<details>
The PKGBUILD defines sources using standard practices: the LICENSE file is fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com (a GitHub content delivery domain), and architecture-specific binaries are downloaded from the project's GitHub releases page. The `source` array entries use direct HTTPS URLs pointing to the declared upstream (`$url`, which resolves to a vernette/warpscout repository). There are no command substitutions, eval statements, or executable payloads in the global scope or within `pkgver()`. The `pkgver` is hardcoded and does not execute external commands.

Checksums are provided via `b2sums` for all sources, including per-architecture variants, which ensures integrity verification during source download. Although the LICENSE file is pulled from a mutable branch (master), this is low-risk as it is not executed and only used for licensing information. No code is executed during sourcing of the PKGBUILD; the only operations are variable assignments and array definitions.

The commands `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` will safely fetch and verify sources without executing any build or prepare steps. There is no evidence of malicious behavior such as data exfiltration, remote code execution, or unauthorized network activity during PKGBUILD sourcing.
</details>

</security_assessment>

The `.SRCINFO` file defines metadata for the `warpscout-bin` package, which is a binary release of a Cloudflare WARP endpoint scanner. It specifies sources from trusted domains: the LICENSE file is fetched from `raw.githubusercontent.com` under the project's official repository, and the prebuilt binaries for aarch64 and x86_64 are downloaded directly from GitHub Releases at `github.com/vernette/warpscout`. All sources are from the official and expected domain for the project.

Checksums are provided using b2sum (BLAKE2), a cryptographically secure hash function, and match the respective sources. This ensures integrity of the downloaded binaries and license file. The package does not use `git clone` or include mutable VCS operations like `git pull`, which could introduce unchecked code at build time. Instead, it pulls fixed-version release artifacts, which is a safe practice for `-bin` packages.

There are no signs of obfuscated URLs, unexpected network destinations, or scripts that could exfiltrate data or execute arbitrary code. The package follows standard AUR packaging conventions for a binary distribution. While checksums are not 'SKIP', they are present and specific to each architecture, enhancing trust in the sources. No malicious behavior is evident.
</details>

The license file is also fetched from the master branch, but this is low-risk as it is only installed to `/usr/share/licenses/` and not executed.

While the source URL for the LICENSE uses an unversioned branch (master), this is not a security concern because the file is not used in the build process and license files are not security-sensitive in the same way as code. All executable components are versioned and checksummed. No obfuscated code, unexpected file operations, or data exfiltration mechanisms are present.

<details>
This PKGBUILD is safe for the narrow gate of running `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo`.

The `source` arrays reference only the package's own upstream GitHub project (github.com/vernette/warpscout) for the prebuilt release tarballs, plus the raw.githubusercontent.com mirror of the project's LICENSE file. No `pkgver()` function exists, so nothing executes during that step either. The `package()` function is not reached under `--nobuild`/`--noprepare`, and in any event it contains only standard `install` commands into `$pkgdir`.

B2 checksums are provided for all three sources. Even if they were `SKIP`, downloading and extracting archives for later audit is precisely what these commands are designed to do, so that alone would never fail this gate. Fetching from the project's own upstream is expected packaging behavior. The only minor hygiene note is that the LICENSE source tracks the unpinned `master` branch, which is a supply-chain reproducibility consideration but not malicious.
</details>
